title: pcapng: Added dissection of Darwin process information, as collected by...
description:
pcapng: Added dissection of Darwin process information, as collected by "tcpdump -k" on Darwin machines.

Following the discussion on the dev mailing list https://lists.wireshark.org/archives/wireshark-dev/202504/msg00015.html, this MR adds to Wireshark the ability to dissect the *legacy* process information and metadata.

# Context (it is easy to get lost in the long discussion):

About 13 years ago, Apple added the flag `-k` to the `tcpdump` that ships with all Darwin-based operating systems. The flag allows associating packets with the process that holds the 5-tuple, as well as outputting various debugging metadata, mostly useful for chasing delays and otherwise debugging the protocols stacks.

It is highly desirable to expose this information to Wireshark, so that an engineer who faces a difficult problem could:
1. Identify the chatty processes.
2. Identify "wake packets", which would cause the modem/WLAN to wake the operating system, those are a major factor in energy saving.
3. Use different trace facilities to correlate the traffic patterns as observed on the network with the process activities as observed via other tools.

Today, it is possible to view the information when using the MIME encoding. It is *not* possible, though to use the information in the context of packet dissection.

## Backwards compatibility, ossification and disambiguation 

When the new options were added, the pcapng specification did not include the support for the custom blocks. As a result, Apple used the only extension mechanism that was available at the time, which is the "local" blocks/options. Unfortunately, the "local" blocks are reserved for non-public software which is specific to companies; e.g. if Acme Inc. decides to implement support for RFC2549 (QoS for IP over Avian Carriers), it could use the "local" blocks to convey the information on the said Avian Carriers. Sadly, if Acme Inc. decides to do so, its custom blocks will collide, with high probability, with the de-facto standard options used by billions of devices that has been running Darwin for the last decade.

Today, the pcapng specification supports extensions via custom blocks, which use the IANA PEN (private enterprise number) for registration. It would make sense for Apple to update `tcpdump` to use the custom blocks, so that in the future collisions could be avoided. This leaves, however, the question of supporting the existing pcap files that has been collected over the years.

## Design choices
While not pretending to have made the best choices, I still would like to call those out explicitly:

### Disambiguating options: Plugins, then Darwin
This MR assumes that the only mechanism to use the local block/option numbers which would potentially collide with the Apple metadata is via plugins. Furthermore, this MR follows the principle of specificity: if Wireshark instance loads a plugin, which is going to use the local block/option numbers, the data should be handled by the plugin. Otherwise, the data is handled by the core Wireshark, reflecting the "quasi-standard" status of the Apple extensions.

### Exposing information to `pinfo`
#### Process information : Indirect access, similar to the interface information
Following the discussion in https://lists.wireshark.org/archives/wireshark-dev/202504/msg00015.html, I decided to take example of interface id/names for handling the process information:
1. The `pinfo` objects hold the `interface_id`.
2. When needed, the interface information can be queried via `epan_get_interface_name` et. al., which would dispatch the call to the particular set of callbacks that are appropriate for the application (Wireshark, tshark, rawshark, etc.)

To that extent, I added the functions `epan_get_process_name`, `epan_get_process_uuid` that act similarly to the `epan_get_interface_name` et. al.

#### Packet metadata: Direct access, similar to how other metadata is stored.
For now, I have added a structure member to the `pinfo`, which holds all the Darwin-specific information. I opted for the most straightforward implementation, but I am open for feedback on a potentially better place for it.

3. For the Wireshark, to be able to dissect the information both in the current ossified form (this MR), and in the future *desired* form(s), as well as any combination of the two.

> "PEN attribution" in what sense?

I am not sure I used the best terminology here. What I meant to say is that it is my *desire* that in the future, Darwin tcpdump will move away from using the LOCAL blocks / options, but will be using CUSTOM blocks / options, while using the PEN==63. By *attribution* I meant that the CUSTOM blocks can be attributed to the PEN without any ambiguity or risk of collision.

> For the Darwin tcpdump to continue adding new metadata, beyond what it does today, while using the portable format (CUSTOM blocks/options vs. LOCAL).

Apple owns everything after the 0x00000BAD/0x40000BAD, block length, and 63 in your Custom Block, and everything after the 2989/19373, option length, and 63 in your binary-data Custom Option.

This means, for example, that you can follow it with an integral value that corresponds to a particular type of Custom Block or binary Custom Option, and use different values for different block or option types; you just need a mechanism *inside Apple* to keep different people from using the same value for different purposes - given that you own the PEN of 63, you don't need to worry about anybody else (or, at least, anybody else who  doesn't go beyond what the pcapng specification says) causing a collision.

> For the Wireshark, to be able to dissect the information both in the current ossified form (this MR), and in the future _desired_ form(s), as well as any combination of the two.

Wireshark - and any other application reading captures with a Custom Block or Custom Option - can be extended to handle particular local blocks and options and custom blocks and options with particular PENs. (I'm in the process of adding plugin mechanisms for that.) If you use an integral value in your Custom Block and binary Custom Option, the Wireshark code (and equivalent code in other programs) can use the integral values I mentioned to distinguish between different current - and future - uses for that block and option.

It can handle any mixture of local and custom blocks and any mixture of local blocks and options.

> By _attribution_ I meant that the CUSTOM blocks can be attributed to the PEN without any ambiguity or risk of collision.

There's no ambiguity about [the private enterprise numbers listing](https://www.iana.org/assignments/enterprise-numbers/enterprise-numbers) - each PEN is assigned to a particular enterprise. PEN 15, for example, is assigned to Xylogics; it presumably now belongs to whatever enterprise has it following Nortel's bankruptcy.

Unless either 1) the IANA screws up and assigns 63 to somebody else (extremely unlikely, I suspect) or 2) somebody steals PEN 63 for their own purposes (in which case, all complaints by that somebody will be dismissed by the Wireshark developers in favor of Apple, and Apple are recommended to refer the thief to the reply given in Arkell v. @guyharris @AndersBroman @alagoutte @jim.young do you have any concerns or comments?

I've been hoping for some type of direct support in Wireshark for accessing the Apple meta data for a very long time. This patch accomplishes that. My current concern is that any edits of an Apple generated pcapng file (using the Wireshark tools, such as adding packet comments, modifying time stamps, saving a copy or exporting a subset) results in the silent loss Apple's process info block and the various Apple EPB options in the updated or newly created pcapng file.

That would require that custom blocks that don't show up in the list ("internal") be added to a list maintained by wiretap - just as, for example, interface information from IDBs does - and be written out.

For IDBs, there is no significance defined for their position in a file - it's not as if an IDB appearing in the middle is guaranteed to be a signal that the interface appeared at that time - so they can all be moved to the beginning of the output file without loss of information.

Is that the case for Process Information Blocks?

> For IDBs, there is no significance defined for their position in a file

There is no significance for their position in a section. If there's more than one section, wiretap (and also dumpcap when generating its own SHBs from multiple inputs) moves them all to the start and reduces down to one section and rewrites the interfaces as necessary. Unfortunately this doesn't quite work with Simple Packet Blocks - while it's able to figure out which interface the SPB refers to, that's not true about the timestamp, but there's no packet block type for "has an interface ID, not necessarily the first interface, but doesn't have a timestamp." So ex SPBs become EPBs with a nonsense timestamp. But that's perhaps a pcapng issue.

@jim.young Agree this is a needed functionality; I can add it to this MR (once there's a consensus on what is the best approach), or alternatively I can follow up with a subsequent MR. It is really a question of "best practice", and I don't know what is the Wireshark "best practice" in this regard.

@guyharris I think there's potential problem with moving all Legacy PIBs into a single section. The Legacy PIBs do not have a stable identifier; instead the options in EPBs are referring to PIBs using the order in which the PIBs appear in the section. 

Because of that, ~~reordering~~ moving all PIBs to be in the beginning of the section would work correctly; but moving all PIBs into a separate section would not.

This also highlights the need for a stable identifier in the "New Style PIBs" (v.s. the legacy PIBs), so that those could be moved between the sections.

Edit: initially I wrote "reordering", but "reordering" would be a problem; moving all PIBs to the beginning of a section *while preserving the order* would be fine.

@guyharris other than the section, the Legacy PIBs are not events and therefore can all be moved to the beginning of the section.

Edit: clarified that I am referring to the Legacy PIBs here.

> I think there's potential problem with moving all Legacy PIBs into a single section.

Sorry, I didn’t make it clear that the stored IDBs are stored per-*section*, and that the same would be true for the stored PIBs.
@guyharris ah, ok, then the "section-specificity" of the PIBs would not be a problem. All PIBs can be safely moved to the beginning of the section, as long as the order is preserved.

So probably wiretap would be better off not combining sections when saving? Combining sections is the default behavior when merging as well.

I am not sure how dumpcap reading from multiple piped interfaces which have PIBs would work either, since it also reduces sections to one (this doesn't happen with a single interface, which passes through.)

For IDBs, in some of those situations the Interface ID is rewritten in all the packets so that it's consistent. I don't know if a similar rewriting would work for PIBs.

@johnthacker I think that the compatibility state machine should be something akin to
```
+------------------------------+         +------------------------------+
|  Legacy PIB format           |         |  New PIB format              |
|  Can be opened by:           |         |  Can be opened by:           |
|  1. Wireshark (ver: 4.5? +)  |         |  1. Wireshark (ver: 4.5? +)  |
|  2. Darwin tcpdump (all vers)|         |  2. Darwin tcpdump (future v)|
|                              |         |                              |
|       +------------------+   |         |       +------------------+   |
|       |  Original file   |---+-upgrade-+------>|  Original file   |   |
|       +------------------+   |         |       +------------------+   |
|                 |            |         |                 |            |
|               edit           |         |               edit           |
|                 v            |         |                 v            |
|         +---------------+    |         |         +---------------+    |
|         |  Edited file  |----+-upgrade-+-------->|  Edited file  |    |
|         +---------------+    |         |         +---------------+    |
|                              |         |                              |
+------------------------------+         +------------------------------+
```

which means that once the pcapng with Legacy PIBs has been edited by Wireshark, it should still be openable by Darwin tcpdump (all versions). Apple only maintains software 7 versions back, which means that from the point of view of any Darwin tcpdump versions, the PIBs have been present from the origin of time.

and likewise, the once the "proper PIB" blocks will have been defined, those should be openable by both Wireshark (starting from some version) and Darwin tcpdump (from some ver.)

From this point of view, if the sections will be rewritten, it would be highly desirable for the Darwin tcpdump to be able to open those.

@johnthacker from this point of view, if we have lets say 2 sections with PIBs, and we want dumpcap to combine the PIBs into a single section as well as to rewrite the EPBs that reference the PIBs, the question will be whether the existing tcpdump will be able to open the file and to reference the PIBs. I don't have an answer to that question, but I will try to figure it out.

@mmann78 it is a bit more complicated. Two separate mechanisms are required to handle the Darwin metadata.

The first mechanism (let's call it "legacy") needs to address the *current* situation, where the Darwin metadata is using the LOCAL block id space. This is what this MR is trying to accomplish.

The second mechanism (let's call it "future") needs to address the *desired* situation, where the Darwin metadata is using the CUSTOM block id space. The "future" mechanism is out of scope of this MR; a new MR should be created once Darwin tcpdump has been updated and shipped.

As far as I can tell, the changes in !19841 and in !19781 are not helping much for the "legacy" mechanism. Let's say the "legacy" mechanism is implemented by registering a plugin to handle the "legacy" data. Let's also say that some 3rd party developer decides to use a LOCAL block id for their own purposes, and implements a plugin (let's call it "third-party"). In this situation, how should a block with id `0x80000001` be handled?

The desired behavior seems to have the block with id `0x80000001` to be handled by a "third-party" plugin, if it is installed and is claiming the block id; otherwise the block should be handled by the "legacy" mechanism for handling Darwin metadata.

Unless I am missing something, the mechanism proposed in !19841 does not support the disambiguation of the blocks with ids in the LOCAL id space.

The idea behind !19841 is to better abstract handling of "any" block type and to limit the definition of "internal" block. I see an "internal" block as any block type \< 0x100 (per pcapng spec) and 0x00000BAD and 0x40000BAD.  All others should be able to follow the "plugin" format (with registration), whether they are a "plugin" or "built in" (just like dissectors).  !19841 converts the sysdig functionality from "internal" to "built in".  The main reason it hasn't been merged is there isn't a good way to distinguish "proper registration" (like sysdig did) and "someone arbitrarily picking a non-local type" (which we want to discourage).  I don't want block handlers to have to modify wiretap code for "yes I have registered the block ID I want to use" in addition to registering their block(s) so it passes the current checks (that's currently why !19841 doesn't work).  They should just be able to call (newly updated) register_pcapng_block_type_handler().

If I understand it correctly, I would like "legacy" Darwin functionality to function as a "built in" - with one exception.  !19841 behaves as "first come, first serve", the idea being "built-ins" (that probably registered their block IDs) get preference over plugins.  I'm okay with explicitly adding the exception of a plugin being able to override the "built in" 0x80000001 "legacy" Darwin functionality. So pcapng-darwin-custom.c should have a call to register_pcapng_block_type_handler(), but then also have the "allowed to override 0x80000001" functionality in register_pcapng_block_type_handler().

The (selfish) reason I wanted !19841 merged before this patch is I didn't want to have to handle the merge conflicts and converting Darwin "legacy" functionality into "built in", similar to what's done to sysdig.  (Hopefully your 2 week gap is enough time to have !19841 be merged so it becomes a non-issue)

@mmann78 I can wait, my employer keeps me beyond busy these days.

My concerns are:
1. We don't want to proliferate the use of 0x8... block ids in built-ins. Apple did not have a choice at the time, because that was the only option. Now there are better options. So.. make the desirable behavior easy, and undesirable behavior hard. 
2. Despite the Darwin blocks options being 0x8..., they are essentially an ossified custom block, since it has been around for 13 years. So in this sense those are exceptions.
3. Finally, we have what I call "elevator problem". If one were to look at the histogram of the floors used, the "ground" will be the most used by far. In a similar way, there is a much higher probability of collision for the low IDs in the local block space (i.e. `0x80000001`, `0x8000002` etc.) than in the middle of the range (e.g. `0x800a0001`, `0x800a0002`). And Darwin uses `0x8000001`, practically inviting collisions. In the case of collision, the *locally installed* plugin should win. If there is no *locally installed* plugin that claims the contested block ids, I would like the Darwin thing to be the default, because it is used by more than a billion devices. 


So once the "allow to override" or similar semantics are figured out, I don't mind moving the Darwin code away from the pcapng. What I do want is to have the Darwin thing to be available everywhere, without the need to install the plugin, and to be the default, unless a *locally installed* plugin claims the blocks. And finally, I want to have the code to clearly state that "hey, Darwin did it because at the time there was no other way. Today there is other way. Don't use the `0x8....` block id space if what you really want is the CUSTOM block". Because existing code always provides kind of a guidance to the developers that come after, and as I said earlier - I do believe that the approach of "make the desirable behavior easy, make the undesirable behavior difficult" works.

Initially I thought that the process information is sort of different, because we have the process concept on many different systems not just Darwin.

##### Thoughts on the process information (name, id)

The process information seems to me something that is universal for every UNIX/UNIXish system, and somewhat supported by other systems as well. At the moment, I don't know about any UNIX except for Darwin that can provide the process information in the pcap, but it seems plausible that a "process information" will be available on a large number of different systems. Would it make more sense to have `darwin.process.id` / `darwin.process.name` vs. `frame.process.id` / `frame.process.name` ? To me it seems that the process information abstraction is similar to the interface name abstraction, and belongs to the frame.

In any way, my opinions on the process Id/ process name placement are weakly held. I will be happy if the process id / process name will go to Darwin layer; I will be likely happy if it will go to the `frame` layer. I have added the above reasoning only to make my thought process (however biased it may be) clear.

##### Thoughts on other Darwin metadata

Unlike the process information, other Darwin metadata is quite specific to Darwin. Things like `wake packet` `nexus`, `droptap` etc. would probably be better kept in a separate dissection layer; I think this the right thing to do here. In other words: I think that all the Darwin metadata that is not part of the above "process information" should be identifiable via `darwin.metadata.flags`, `darwin.drop.reason` etc.

#### Thoughts on DPEB order

> (because the data could come in any order and there are some that are "grouped").

I wonder whether this degree of flexibility is truly needed. It may not be obvious, but the relationship between the DPEBs and the EPB blocks that reference those is quite fragile:

1. The DPEBs do not have a stable identifier. There is a "process UUID", but that's UUID of the process, not of the DPEB.
2. The EPBs reference the DPEBs based on the order in which the DPEBs appear in the file.

Because of this scheme (of which I am not fond of, to say the least, but this is the reality), the Darwin tcpdump will _always_ put the DPEB block before any frame that references it; this allows for a single-pass reading.

Will that relationship survive file edits? I believe the relationship will trivially survive operations that remove EPBs (such as `"Export Specified Packets` in the `Export` Wireshark dialog or `tshark -r input.pcapng -w output.pcapng -Y filter_expression`), but will require more work for operations that add EPBs (e.g. `mergecap`):

##### Operations that remove packets

To maintain the relationships, operations that remove EPBs will need to pass-through the DPEB blocks. If all DPEBs are just kept around, then:

1. The relative order of DPEBs will not change.
2. All EPBs that reference a particular DPEB will appear after the said DPEB.
3. Because no DPEB is removed, the EPB options will not have to be updated, at all.

Consider the below illustration, which has 3 DPEBs that represent 3 different processes, and are referenced by 3 different packet groups (marked by blue, yellow and red in the illustration below). Once the "yellow" EPBs are removed, the second DPEB becomes orphaned, but the integrity of the file won't be affected.

![Screenshot 2025-06-02 at 6.44.01 PM.png](/uploads/76238e75932a32896be90ecbfd7ea354/Screenshot_2025-06-02_at_6.44.01_PM.png){width="473" height="369"}

This may sound wasteful, but there are in reality very few DPEBs even in pcapng files with many millions of packets. Recall that a DPEB is only written to a file if the writing tcpdump process hasn't created a DPEB before, so those are essentially unique.

##### Operations that add packets

Operations such as `mergecap` would need to make multiple passes to update the references. Consider the below illustration. Before the two pcapng files are merged, both have "first" DPEB, but once merged one of the "firsts" will become "second", and so on.

It's really *neither*.  An "event" corresponds to an event happening on whatever is the source of packets etc., e.g. "carrier lost".  A "report" corresponds to a report of information as of the time it was reported, e.g. "here are packet capture statistics as of now". Both are often time-stamped. The difference is that the time difference between, say, the arrival of a packet, or the loss of carrier, or..., and an event in the past, may be significant, but the time difference between a report in the past and a packet etc. is less likely to be significant. (What this *really* illustrates is that "delta from previous packet", in a world where not everything in the "packet" list is necessarily a packet, needs to be rethought. Either it should *strictly* refer to packets, or perhaps needs to be configurable.)

The process blocks are more like descriptions, similar to Interface Description Blocks; they just say "here's information about a process that received or sent packets", so that packets can be marked as being received or sent by that process, just as an IDB says "here's information about an interface on which packets were received or sent", so that packets can be marked as being received or sent on that interface.

Addressed an issue where some DPEB blocks did not have `end-of-option` marker.

The issue was in the discrepancy between how the option size was calculated, and how the options were populated.

When calculating the size of the DPEB options block, the code used

```
    options_size = pcapng_compute_options_size(sdata, compute_dpeb_option_size);
```

The function `pcapng_compute_options_size` (via the function `compute_block_option_size`) opts to silently omit options with zero size.

On the other hand, when writing the options block, the code used 

```
    wtap_block_foreach_option(sdata, put_dpeb_option, &opt_ptr);
```

The function `put_dpeb_option` _did not_ omit options with zero size.

When the process name in the DPEB block is not empty, this discrepancy did not have any effect. However, the process name was empty, this discrepancy caused the result of `wtap_block_foreach_option(...)` to write the option header for the empty string, in effect using up the 4 bytes that the function `pcapng_compute_options_size` reserved for the `end-of-options` marker. As a result, the `end-of-options` marker was not written.

At the moment, this MR is following the choices made by `compute_block_option_size`, i.e.: when the process name has zero length, the corresponding option is neither accounted for the size computation (because of how the pcapng code is written), nor for populating the options block (because I am specifically omitting the empty process names when writing). So far it seems to work: both Wireshark and the Darwin tcpdump are able to read the files with the process name missing.

commits_data.title: pcapng: Added dissection of Darwin metadata
commits_data.message:
pcapng: Added dissection of Darwin metadata

On Darwin-based systems, running `tcpdump -k` will collect useful
metadata, including:
 - Process information (pid, name, etc.)
 - Packet metadata (Wake, Retry, First packet in flow, etc.)
 - The id of the flow the packet belongs to
 - Trace tag, which can be set by the kernel

 In addition, if `tcpdump` is using the `droptap` pseudo-interface
 for capturing packet that were dropped by the kernel, the metadata will
 include:
 - The drop reason code (for now, opaque)
 - The function name that dropped the packet (not always present)
 - The line number of the callsite of the packet drop (likewise, not always
   present)

These abilities were added to Darwin `tcpdump` about 13 years ago, and
at the time the pcapng format did not support custom blocks that can be
attributed to companies via the Private Enterprise Number (PEN).

Because of that, Darwin `tcpdump` uses the "local" codes for the block
that stores the process information, as well as for the EPB options that
describe the metadata, or refer to the previously mentioned blocks.

This presents a problem, since the "local" codes can be used by
3rd-party plugins.

In order to disambiguate the meaning of the "local" codes, the plugins
are given priority in processing the pcapng block data. If no plugin
claims the "local" codes, the block data is assumed to belong to Darwin
systems.

In the future the disambiguation mechanism can be enhanced, e.g. via
preferences, but at the moment it is kept simple.

Currently, the MR supports reading and writing DPEB information, but not
merging.
